name: Tenant electricity (Mieterstrom)
summary: A landlord or contractor installs rooftop PV on an apartment building and sells the power directly to tenants, who still get a grid supply for the rest.
how_it_makes_money: Sale of on-site solar power to tenants at a price below grid supply, plus a federal tenant electricity surcharge and savings on certain levies and grid charges.

hardware: Metering that separates solar from grid power
regulation: German tenant electricity rules and surcharge
data: Metered production and consumption per tenant

stakeholder_value.provider: Revenue from tenant supply and surcharge
stakeholder_value.other: Landlord gets a use for the roof

what_must_be_true: Building is large enough for the project to break even
Smart metering can separate solar and grid power

risks_failure_causes.text: Restrictive legal framework and high transaction costs are the main barrier found in expert interviews
Projects on buildings with fewer than 20 residential units tend not to be profitable (Berlin evaluation)
Developers cannot be sure how many tenants will participate; tenants show inertia in switching
In existing buildings smart meters that separate solar and grid power often cannot be installed or cost too much

cases.note: The scheme has been in place since 2017 yet only about 1 percent of its annual budget had been claimed by 2021, and as of April 2024 only about 9,000 PV systems existed on apartment buildings.
74 PV tenant electricity projects with 12.6 MWp were in operation at the end of 2020.

Went through preliminary insolvency proceedings at the turn of the year; the operating business moved to a new company on 1 January 2026, and the tenant electricity business is being handed over to partners such as Polarstern while it focuses on building modernisation strategies.

sources.title: Moser et al. (2021): Solar prosumers in the German energy transition (Energies 14(4))
